summary: Allows Anycast-RP to be used inside a domain that runs only PIM. Other multicast protocols, such as MSDP, which has traditionally solved this problem, are not required. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If several helpers all share one name, you can call whichever is closest. This makes that work for multicast without extra helpers.

subtitle: How PIM routers can share one Rendezvous Point address across several routers without needing MSDP.

tldr.problem: Anycast-RP gives fast recovery when a PIM Rendezvous Point fails, but the RPs must learn about each other's sources, a job traditionally done by MSDP.
tldr.mechanism: An RP that receives a PIM Register from a designated router sends a copy of it to every other RP in the Anycast-RP set, using its own address as the source.
tldr.outcome: Anycast-RP works inside a PIM-only domain with less protocol machinery, though MSDP may still be needed to talk to other domains.

today: RFC 4610 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Anycast-RP Without MSDP
sections.content:
Anycast-RP, as described in RFC 3446, is a mechanism ISP backbones have used to get fast convergence when a PIM Rendezvous Point (RP) router fails. For receivers and sources to meet at the closest RP, packets from a source need to reach all RPs so they can find joined receivers.

That is the source discovery problem MSDP was meant to solve. This memo instead extends the PIM Register mechanism so Anycast-RP functionality is kept without MSDP.
sections.eli5: Normally a separate messenger service tells every helper about new senders. This idea lets the helpers pass the news along themselves.

sections.title: Setting Up the Anycast-RP Set
sections.content:
The setup has these parts:

  • A unicast IP address is chosen as the RP address, configured statically or distributed by a dynamic protocol to all PIM routers in the domain.
  • A set of routers, the Anycast-RP set, acts as RP for that address. Each has a loopback interface using the RP address.
  • Each router also has a separate IP address for communication between RPs. The RP address must differ from these.
  • The RP address, or a covering prefix, is injected into unicast routing inside the domain.
  • Each router is configured with the addresses of all other routers in the set, consistently on every RP.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the group wears a name tag with the same shared name, but each also has a private phone number so the group can call each other.

sections.title: How a Register Is Shared
sections.content:
The rules here blend with RFC 4601 and, if there is any question, RFC 4601 takes precedence. When a source S1 starts sending, its designated router (DR) forms a PIM Register message addressed to the Anycast-RP address, and unicast routing delivers it to the nearest RP, say RP1. RP1 decapsulates it and sends the packet down the shared tree to its receivers.

Because the Register did not come from a configured RP, RP1 assumes it came from a DR and sends a copy to every other RP in the set, using its own address as the source. If the Register was not addressed to the Anycast-RP address, an error has occurred and it should be logged with rate limiting. RP1 MAY join the source tree with an (S1,G) Join, but MUST create (S1,G) state. It also sends a Register-Stop to the DR. If the copies are lost, the DR resends Registers when its suppression timer expires.

Each other RP decapsulates the copy and forwards to its own receivers, or discards the packet if none have joined, but still creates (S1,G) state so it can join the source tree quickly later. It replies with a Register-Stop, and RP1 takes no specific action on those. An RP MAY delay its Register-Stop until it has received data on the source tree. Sources attached to a different RP, such as S3 at RP3, work the same way in reverse.
sections.eli5: The closest helper hears the news first. It tells the sender thanks, then quickly passes the news to every other helper so all of them know.

sections.title: Rules and Guidelines
sections.content:
An RP copies a Register only if it came from an address not in the Anycast-RP list, meaning from a DR. To guard against inconsistently configured sets, an implementation MUST copy the TTL from the received Register into the copies. DR logic is unchanged; only RPs change, and only in sending copies. Register-Stop processing is unchanged, though an implementation MAY suppress Register-Stop in response to a Register received from an RP. Rate limiting is end to end, DR to RP to the other RPs.

Null Registers MUST be replicated to all RPs in the set so source state stays alive. The set should stay small to keep non-native replication low. An RP that does not support this specification can be mixed in, but should not have sources registering to it, though receivers may join it. Because copies and the Register-Stop go out at the same time, packets can be lost, and state can be missing in other RPs until the DR sends Registers again. Physical RP changes are as fast as unicast route convergence.
sections.eli5: Only the first helper to hear from a sender passes it on, so the news does not bounce around forever. Keep the group small so the whispering stays quick.

sections.title: Interaction with MSDP
sections.content:
The aim is to remove MSDP peering between the Anycast-RPs, but MSDP may still be needed to advertise internal sources outside the PIM domain and to learn external sources. In a stub domain, an Anycast-RP processes Registers both as described here and as RFC 4601 describes, so several RPs might originate a Source-Active (SA) message for the same source. If that is undesirable, only some RPs can be configured for MSDP peering.

If only some RPs have external MSDP peers, those that do must be configured with the set that do not, and the RFC recommends configuring all Anycast-RPs with external MSDP peering to avoid periodic Register traffic. In a transit domain, an Anycast-RP set should not be mixed with MSDP peering among its members, and the document makes no attempt to connect MSDP peering domains together using Anycast-PIM.
sections.eli5: If you need to talk to a different neighbourhood, you may still need the old messenger service for that part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could forge a Register using an address from the Anycast-RP list to overwhelm the target RP, inject unauthorized data to its receivers, or create bogus SA entries in other PIM domains if the RP has external MSDP peerings. A forged Register-Stop has limited effect beyond denial of service, since an RP usually ignores them.

Denial of service with forged messages cannot be prevented, but an RP can rate-limit incoming messages or refuse to process Register-Stop messages. Unauthorized data can be prevented using the method in section 6.3.2 of RFC 4601, where the copying RP acts as the DR and the receiving RP as the RP. Per-member keys cause a key management problem, so where all RPs are under one administrative control, the same authentication parameters, including the key, may be used for all Registered packets.
sections.eli5: A faker could pretend to be one of the helpers and send fake news. Secret passwords help, and sharing one password among the helpers is simpler.
